Follow tracks, forage, find a trail, or avoid natural hazards.

entries.name: Determining Skills
entries: A character's starting skill proficiencies are determined at character creation, and a monster's skill proficiencies appear in its stat block.

entries.name: Skills with Different Abilities
entries: Each skill proficiency is associated with an ability check. For example, the {@skill Intimidation|XPHB} skill is associated with Charisma. In some situations, the DM might allow you to apply your skill proficiency to a different ability check. For example, if a character tries to intimidate someone through a show of physical strength, the DM might ask for a Strength ({@skill Intimidation|XPHB}) check rather than a Charisma ({@skill Intimidation|XPHB}) check. That character would make a Strength check and add their Proficiency Bonus if they have {@skill Intimidation|XPHB} proficiency.

entries.name: Saving Throw Proficiencies
entries: Proficiency in a saving throw lets a character add their Proficiency Bonus to saves that use a particular ability. For example, proficiency in Wisdom saves lets you add your Proficiency Bonus to your Wisdom saves. Some monsters also have saving throw proficiencies, as noted in their stat blocks.

Each class gives proficiency in at least two saving throws, representing that class's training in evading or resisting certain threats. Wizards, for example, are proficient in Intelligence and Wisdom saves; they train to resist mental assault.

entries.name: Equipment Proficiencies
entries: A character gains proficiency with various weapons and tools from their class and background. There are two categories of equipment proficiency:

items.name: Weapons
items.entry: Anyone can wield a weapon, but proficiency makes you better at wielding it. If you have proficiency with a weapon, you add your Proficiency Bonus to attack rolls you make with it.

items.name: Tools
items.entry: If you have proficiency with a tool, you can add your Proficiency Bonus to any ability check you make that uses the tool. If you have Proficiency in the skill that's also used with that check, you have Advantage on the check too. This means you can benefit from both skill proficiency and tool proficiency on the same ability check.

entries.name: Actions
entries: When you do something other than moving or communicating, you typically take an action. The Action table lists the game's main actions, which are defined in more detail in the {@area rules glossary|a8f|x}.

entries.caption: Actions
rows: Attack with a weapon or an {@variantrule Unarmed Strike|XPHB}.
For the rest of the turn, give yourself extra movement equal to your {@variantrule Speed|XPHB}.
Your movement doesn't provoke {@action Opportunity Attack|XPHB} for the rest of the turn.

Until the start of your next turn, attack rolls against you have {@variantrule Disadvantage|XPHB}, and you make Dexterity saving throws with {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB}. You lose this benefit if you have the {@condition Incapacitated|XPHB} condition or if your Speed is 0.
Help another creature's ability check or attack roll, or administer first aid.

Make a Charisma ({@skill Deception|XPHB}, {@skill Intimidation|XPHB}, {@skill Performance|XPHB}, or {@skill Persuasion|XPHB}) or Wisdom ({@skill Animal Handling|XPHB}) check to alter a creature's attitude.
Cast a spell, use a magic item, or use a magical feature.
Prepare to take an action in response to a trigger you define.
Make a Wisdom ({@skill Insight|XPHB}, {@skill Medicine|XPHB}, {@skill Perception|XPHB}, or {@skill Survival|XPHB}) check.
Make an Intelligence ({@skill Arcana|XPHB}, {@skill History|XPHB}, {@skill Investigation|XPHB}, {@skill Nature|XPHB}, or {@skill Religion|XPHB}) check.

entries: Player characters and monsters can also do things not covered by these actions. Many class features and other abilities provide additional action options, and you can improvise other actions. When you describe an action not detailed elsewhere in the rules, the Dungeon Master tells you whether that action is possible and what kind of {@variantrule D20 Test|XPHB} you need to make, if any.

entries.name: One Thing at a Time
entries: The game uses actions to govern how much you can do at one time. You can take only one action at a time. This principle is most important in combat, as explained in "{@area Combat|06b|x}" later in this chapter.

Actions can come up in other situations, too: in a social interaction, you can try to {@action Influence|XPHB} a creature or use the {@action Search|XPHB} action to read the creature's body language, but you can't do both at the same time. And when you're exploring a dungeon, you can't simultaneously use the {@action Search|XPHB} action to look for traps and use the {@action Help|XPHB} action to aid another character who's trying to open a stuck door (with the {@action Utilize|XPHB} action).

entries.name: Bonus Actions
entries: Various class features, spells, and other abilities let you take an additional action on your turn called a Bonus Action. The Cunning Action feature, for example, allows a Rogue to take a Bonus Action. You can take a Bonus Action only when a special ability, a spell, or another feature of the game states that you can do something as a Bonus Action. You otherwise don't have a Bonus Action to take.
You can take only one Bonus Action on your turn, so you must choose which Bonus Action to use if you have more than one available.

You choose when to take a Bonus Action during your turn unless the Bonus Action's timing is specified. Anything that deprives you of your ability to take actions also prevents you from taking a Bonus Action.

entries.name: Reactions
entries: Certain special abilities, spells, and situations allow you to take a special action called a Reaction. A Reaction is an instant response to a trigger of some kind, which can occur on your turn or on someone else's. The {@action Opportunity Attack|XPHB}, described {@area later in this chapter|08b|x}, is the most common type of Reaction.

When you take a Reaction, you can't take another one until the start of your next turn. If the reaction interrupts another creature's turn, that creature can continue its turn right after the Reaction.
In terms of timing, a Reaction takes place immediately after its trigger unless the Reaction's description says otherwise.

entries.name: What Would Your Character Do?
entries: Ask yourself as you play, "What would my character do?" Playing a role involves some amount of getting into another person's head and understanding what motivates them and how those motivations translate into action. In D&D, those actions unfold against the backdrop of a fantastic world full of situations we can only imagine. How does your character react to those situations?
This advice comes with one important caveat: avoid character choices that ruin the fun of the other players and the DM. Choose actions that delight you and your friends.

entries.name: Social Interaction

entries.title: Characters lay on the charm while bartering for magic items with a green hag

entries: During their adventures, player characters meet many different people and face some monsters that would rather talk than fight. In those situations, it's time for social interaction, which takes many forms. For example, you might try to convince a burglar to confess to wrongdoing or try to flatter a guard. The Dungeon Master assumes the roles of any nonplayer characters who are participating.

An NPC's attitude toward your character is {@variantrule Friendly [Attitude]|XPHB|Friendly}, {@variantrule Indifferent [Attitude]|XPHB|Indifferent}, or {@variantrule Hostile [Attitude]|XPHB|Hostile}, as defined in the {@area rules glossary|a8f|x}. Friendly NPCs are predisposed to help, and Hostile ones are inclined to hinder.
Social interactions progress in two ways: through roleplaying and ability checks.

entries.name: Roleplaying
entries: Roleplaying is, literally, the act of playing out a role. In this case, it's you as a player determining how your character thinks, acts, and talks. Roleplaying is part of every aspect of the game, and it comes to the fore during social interactions.
As you roleplay, consider whether you prefer an active approach or a descriptive approach, each of which is described in "{@area Social Interaction Example.|046|x}"

The DM uses an NPC's personality and your character's actions and attitudes to determine how an NPC reacts. A cowardly bandit might buckle under threats of imprisonment. A stubborn merchant refuses to help if the characters badger her. A vain dragon laps up flattery.
When interacting with an NPC, pay attention to the DM's portrayal of the NPC's personality. You might be able to learn an NPC's goals and then use that information to influence the NPC.

If you offer NPCs something they want or play on their sympathies, fears, or goals, you can form friendships, ward off violence, or learn a key piece of information. On the other hand, if you insult a proud warrior or speak ill of a noble's allies, your efforts to convince or deceive will likely fail.

entries.name: Ability Checks
entries: Ability checks can be key in determining the outcome of a social interaction. Your roleplaying efforts can alter an NPC's attitude, but there might still be an element of chance if the DM wants dice to play a role in determining an NPC's response to you. In such situations, the DM will typically ask you to take the {@action Influence|XPHB} action.

Pay attention to your skill proficiencies when thinking of how you will interact with an NPC; use an approach that relies on your group's skill proficiencies. For example, if the group needs to trick a guard into letting them into a castle, the Rogue who is proficient in {@skill Deception|XPHB} should lead the discussion.

entries.name: Social Interaction Example
entries: In this scene, players engage in a social interaction encounter. You and your group determine how similar scenes play out in your adventures.
{@i Four adventurers—Shreeve, Mirabella, Auro, and Gareth—have traveled to the Blood on the Vine tavern in the grim village of Barovia}.

items.name: Jared (as DM):
items.entry: This tavern might have been finely appointed once, but it has grown shoddy with the passage of years. A blazing fire in the hearth barely gives any warmth to the room. You see a man behind the counter, methodically cleaning glasses. Three older women huddle together at one table. And a handsome young man sits by himself at a corner table, sipping a glass of wine. He looks up as you enter, but the other people ignore you. "Welcome to Barovia," he says. He holds a coin toward the bartender: "A pitcher for the visitors." The glint of silver catches the server's attention.

items.name: Maeve (as Mirabella):
items.entry: "Thank you, friend. May we know to whom we're indebted?"

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: "I am Ismark Kolyanovich, though around here, I am often called Ismark the Lesser."

items.name: Russell (as Shreeve):
items.entry: "That's unfortunate."

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: "Indeed. I hope one day to live up to my father's example and rid myself of that title. And so, my new friends, who are you?"

items.name: Amy (as Auro):
items.entry: "I'm Auro."

items.name: Russell:
items.entry: "Shreeve."

items.name: Phillip (as Gareth):
items.entry: "My name is Gareth."

items.name: Maeve (as Mirabella):
items.entry: "I'm called Mirabella. You said your name was Kolyanovich. Are you related to Kolyan Indirovich, the burgomaster of this town?"

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: He looks a little surprised. He says, "Kolyan Indirovich is my esteemed father, yes."

items.name: Maeve:
items.entry: "Then he's the one who summoned us!" I show him the letter that drew us here.

items.name: Phillip:
items.entry: I watch his reaction as he reads it.

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: He reaches for the letter but pulls back before touching it. "That seal—it's not my father's." Gareth, make a Wisdom (Insight) check.

items.name: Phillip:
items.entry: Gareth got 18.

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: You notice that Ismark is trying to conceal his terror. He's afraid to even touch the letter's seal.

items.name: Phillip:
items.entry: I ask him what's frightening him.

items.name: Russell:
items.entry: "Yeah, whose seal is it?"

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: "The Devil Strahd."

items.name: Amy:
items.entry: "Sounds like a pleasant fellow."

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: "No! He is the vampire lord of Castle Ravenloft and a plague to my sister. You must help her!"

entries.name: Active Roleplaying
entries: Notice throughout the example how Russell and Amy actively roleplay their characters' behavior. In this active approach, they speak with their characters' voices, like an actor taking on a role. The players might even echo their characters' body language. They still need to describe things that can't reasonably be acted out.

entries.name: Descriptive Roleplaying
entries: Notice how Phillip describes his character's words and action. Drawing on his mental image of his character, he says what his character does and how the character does it. If this approach is most comfortable for you, keep these things in mind:

items: Describe your character's emotions and attitude.
Focus on your character's intent and how others might perceive it.
Provide as much embellishment as you feel comfortable with.

entries: Don't worry about getting things exactly right. Focus on what your character would do, and describe what you see in your mind.

entries.name: (1)—Ability Checks
entries: Phillip's character, Gareth, makes a Wisdom ({@skill Insight|XPHB}) check to determine whether he reads Ismark's unspoken cues. Wisdom is the ability that measures perceptiveness and intuition. Insight reflects a character's skill at reading other people's moods and intentions. The DM set the DC at 15, which Gareth beats. With a successful Wisdom ({@skill Insight|XPHB}) check, Gareth gleans information that wasn't obvious, so it wasn't part of the DM's earlier narration. For more information, see "{@area Ability Scores|01c|x}" and "{@area Proficiency|036|x}" earlier in this chapter and the {@action Search|XPHB} action in the {@area rules glossary|a8f|x}.

items.name: Amy:
items.entry: "So Strahd wrote this letter, pretending to be the burgomaster, imploring us to come to Barovia and rescue Ireena Kolyana from a deadly affliction... which is him? Why would he do that?"

items.name: Russell:
items.entry: "Why would he want us to come here?"

items.name: Maeve:
items.entry: "Clearly, he doesn't think we're a threat."

items.name: Amy:
items.entry: "Well, he hasn't met us yet!"

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: "He's toying with you. He delights in the destruction of all things good, like my dear sister."

items.name: Phillip:
items.entry: Gareth draws closer and compassionately asks Ismark whether his sister has been bitten by the vampire.

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: Please make a Charisma (Persuasion) check to see how well he responds to your pastoral manner. You have Advantage because he's Friendly.

items.name: Phillip:
items.entry: Oh, good thing. My first roll was a 7, but with Advantage... ugh, not much better. Well, 10 plus 5 is 15.

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: Ismark leans toward you, Gareth, with a suspicious glance at the other people in the tavern, like he's worried they're eavesdropping. He whispers, "The Devil Strahd desires to make Ireena his latest plaything. Twice he has visited her in the night, using his devilry to secure an invitation into the house—for he can't enter where he isn't invited. Twice he has bitten her, yet she clings to life. But I fear she won't survive another visit!"

items.name: Russell:
items.entry: "All right, Ismark. You bought us drinks and told us about the Devil Strahd and your sister. How can we help?"

entries.name: (2)—Influencing NPCs
entries: Gareth takes the {@action Influence|XPHB} action, which characters can take to influence an NPC. It's easier to influence an NPC who's already disposed to help you, as Ismark is here. Ismark's {@variantrule Friendly [Attitude]|XPHB|Friendly} attitude gives Phillip Advantage on the roll. In this case, {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} made the difference between success and failure.

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: "You are too kind! First, I need your help transporting Ireena to the town of Vallaki."

items.name: Maeve:
items.entry: "Where's Vallaki?"

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: "It lies to the northwest, in the heart of the valley. As the raven flies, it is less than ten miles, but the road winds among the hills and woods, and the journey takes at least five hours at speed."

items.name: Russell:
items.entry: "And why there?"

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: "The town lies beyond the view of Castle Ravenloft, so I hope it's beyond Strahd's spies. And I have heard that Vallaki is well defended, with a wooden palisade and iron gates."

items.name: Russell:
items.entry: "As if such defenses would stop a vampire."

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: "Indeed. But if moving her there can keep him away from her for even a few days, we have time for the second part of our task."

items.name: Russell:
items.entry: "A part where you help us?"

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: "Yes, when I help you face the vampire!"

entries.name: Exploration
entries: Exploration involves delving into places that are dangerous and full of mystery. The rules in this section detail some of the ways adventurers interact with the environment in such places.

entries.name: Adventuring Equipment
entries: As adventurers explore, their equipment can help them in many ways. For example, they can reach out-of-the-way places with a Ladder, perceive things they wouldn't otherwise notice with a Torch or another light source, bypass locked doors and containers with {@item Thieves' Tools|XPHB}, and create obstacles for pursuers with {@item Caltrops|XPHB}.

See {@area chapter 6|63c|x} for rules on many items that are useful on adventures. The items in that chapter's "{@area Tools|65c|x}" and "{@area Adventuring Gear|6a8|x}" sections are especially useful. The weapons in that chapter can also be used for more than battle; you could use a {@item Quarterstaff|XPHB}, for example, to push a sinister-looking button that you're reluctant to touch.

entries.name: Vision and Light
entries: Some adventuring tasks—such as noticing danger, hitting an enemy, and targeting certain spells—are affected by sight, so effects that obscure vision can hinder you, as explained below.

entries.name: Obscured Areas
entries: An area might be Lightly or Heavily Obscured. In a Lightly Obscured area—such as an area with Dim Light, patchy fog, or moderate foliage—you have {@variantrule Disadvantage|XPHB} on Wisdom ({@skill Perception|XPHB}) checks that rely on sight.
A Heavily Obscured area—such as an area with Darkness, heavy fog, or dense foliage—is opaque. You have the {@condition Blinded|XPHB} condition when trying to see something there.

entries.name: Light
entries: The presence or absence of light determines the category of illumination in an area, as defined below.

entries.name: Bright Light
entries: Bright Light lets most creatures see normally. Even gloomy days provide Bright Light, as do torches, lanterns, fires, and other sources of illumination within a specific radius.

entries.name: Dim Light
entries: Dim Light, also called shadows, creates a {@variantrule Lightly Obscured|XPHB} area. An area of Dim Light is usually a boundary between Bright Light and surrounding Darkness. The soft light of twilight and dawn also counts as Dim Light. A full moon might bathe the land in Dim Light.

entries.name: Darkness
entries: Darkness creates a {@variantrule Heavily Obscured|XPHB} area. Characters face Darkness outdoors at night (even most moonlit nights), within the confines of an unlit dungeon, or in an area of magical Darkness.

entries.name: Special Senses
entries: Some creatures have special senses that help them perceive things in certain situations. The rules glossary defines the following special senses:

entries.name: Hiding
entries: Adventurers and monsters often hide, whether to spy on one another, sneak past a guardian, or set an ambush. The Dungeon Master decides when circumstances are appropriate for hiding. When you try to hide, you take the {@action Hide|XPHB} action.

entries.name: Interacting with Objects
entries: Interacting with objects is often simple to resolve. The player tells the DM that their character is doing something, such as moving a lever or opening a door, and the DM describes what happens. Sometimes, however, rules govern what you can do with an object, as detailed in the following sections.

entries.name: What Is an Object?
entries: For the purpose of the rules, an object is a discrete, inanimate item like a window, door, sword, book, table, chair, or stone. It isn't a building or a vehicle, which are composed of many objects.

entries.name: Time-Limited Object Interactions
entries: When time is short, such as in combat, interactions with objects are limited: one free interaction per turn. That interaction must occur during a creature's movement or action. Any additional interactions require the {@action Utilize|XPHB} action, as explained in "{@area Combat|06b|x}" later in this chapter.

entries.name: Finding Hidden Objects
entries: When your character searches for hidden things, such as a secret door or a trap, the DM typically asks you to make a Wisdom ({@skill Perception|XPHB}) check, provided you describe the character searching in the hidden object's vicinity. On a success, you find the object, other important details, or both.
If you describe your character searching nowhere near a hidden object, a Wisdom ({@skill Perception|XPHB}) check won't reveal the object, no matter the check's total.

entries.name: Carrying Objects
entries: You can usually carry your gear and treasure without worrying about the weight of those objects. If you try to haul an unusually heavy object or a massive number of lighter objects, the DM might require you to abide by the rules for {@variantrule carrying capacity|XPHB} in the {@area rules glossary|a8f|x}.

entries.name: Breaking Objects
entries: As an action, you can automatically break or otherwise destroy a fragile, nonmagical object, such as a glass container or a piece of paper. If you try to damage something more resilient, the DM might use the rules on {@variantrule breaking objects|XPHB} in the {@area rules glossary|a8f|x}.

entries.name: Hazards
entries: Monsters are the main perils characters face, but other dangers await. The rules glossary defines the following hazards:

entries.name: Travel
entries: During an adventure, the characters might travel long distances on trips that could take hours or days. The DM can summarize this travel without calculating exact distances or travel times, or the DM might have you use the travel pace rules below.
If you need to know how fast you can move when every second matters, see the movement rules in "{@area Combat|06b|x}" later in this chapter.

entries.name: Marching Order
entries: The adventurers should establish a marching order while they travel, whether indoors or outdoors. A marching order makes it easier to determine which characters are affected by traps, which ones can spot hidden enemies, and which ones are the closest to those enemies if a fight breaks out. You can change your marching order outside combat and record the order any way you like: write it down, for example, or arrange miniatures to show it.

entries.name: Travel Pace
entries: While traveling outside combat, a group can move at a Fast, Normal, or Slow pace, as shown on the Travel Pace table. The table states how far the party can move in a period of time; if riding horses or other mounts, the group can move twice that distance for 1 hour, after which the mounts need a {@variantrule Short Rest|XPHB|Short} or {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB} before they can move at that increased pace again (see {@area chapter 6|6fe|x} for a selection of mounts for sale). The {@i Dungeon Master's Guide} has rules that affect which pace you can choose in certain types of terrain.
Each travel pace has a game effect, as defined below.

entries.name: Fast
entries: Traveling at a Fast pace imposes {@variantrule Disadvantage|XPHB} on a traveler's Wisdom ({@skill Perception|XPHB} or {@skill Survival|XPHB}) and Dexterity ({@skill Stealth|XPHB}) checks.

entries.name: Normal
entries: Traveling at a Normal pace imposes {@variantrule Disadvantage|XPHB} on Dexterity ({@skill Stealth|XPHB}) checks.

entries.name: Slow
entries: Traveling at a Slow pace grants {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} on Wisdom ({@skill Perception|XPHB} or {@skill Survival|XPHB}) checks.

entries.name: Vehicles
entries: Travelers in wagons, carriages, or other land vehicles choose a pace as normal. Characters in a waterborne vessel are limited to the speed of the vessel, and they don't choose a travel pace. Depending on the vessel and the size of the crew, ships might be able to travel for up to 24 hours per day. {@area Chapter 6|6fe|x} includes vehicles for sale.

entries.name: Exploration Example
entries: This scene finds the player characters investigating a mysterious and potentially dangerous location. They're moving through the environment and interacting with things they find there.
{@i The characters are exploring Castle Ravenloft, and the DM describes the room the characters have entered}.

items.name: Jared (as DM):
items.entry: A blazing hearth fire fills this room with warm light. Firelight glints off a poker beside the fireplace, and the walls are lined with ancient books. A huge painting hangs above the mantelpiece in a gilded frame. The firelight illuminates the portrait—an exact likeness of Ireena Kolyana.

items.name: Phillip (as Gareth):
items.entry: How old does the painting look?

items.name: Maeve (as Mirabella):
items.entry: I'm going to check the books!

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: OK, I'll get to those in a second. Russell and Amy, what are your characters doing?

items.name: Russell (as Shreeve):
items.entry: I stand near the door, sword drawn, ready for danger. This place is creepy!

items.name: Amy (as Auro):
items.entry: I go near the fireplace. A warm fire sounds nice. But I'm also alert for danger.

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: Got it. OK, Phillip, please make an Intelligence (History) check as Gareth looks at the painting.

items.name: Phillip:
items.entry: I don't have proficiency in History, but here goes. I got—oh! A 20! For a total of... 20.

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: Two things leap out at Gareth about the painting. First, the woman's clothes look old-fashioned. Second, the paint is flaking in places, and the whole thing is covered by a thin layer of soot. You'd say this painting is a few centuries old.

items.name: Phillip:
items.entry: So maybe an ancestor of Ireena's? Unless she's already a vampire and this "bitten by Strahd" thing is a ruse.

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: Who knows? Now, Mirabella's looking at the books?

items.name: Maeve:
items.entry: Yeah, I pull one off the shelf at random.

entries.name: Everyone Is Accounted For
entries: Exploration is open-ended; the players don't take turns moving around the dungeon the way they do in combat. But the DM frequently checks in to make sure it's clear where everyone is and what they're doing.

entries.name: Teamwork Matters
entries: The player characters are working toward a common goal. They move together through the dungeon and cooperate to overcome its challenges. When the characters enter the room, they explore different parts of the room. When Auro finds a secret door behind the fireplace later in the example, they come together again to examine it, and Gareth figures out how to bypass the fire. It might seem like Russell's character wasn't doing much, but Shreeve was protecting the group by guarding the door.

entries.name: (3)—Worth Rolling with or without Proficiency
entries: You usually have a chance of success on an ability check even if you don't have proficiency in a relevant skill. In the example, Phillip gets a 20 without proficiency. The {@dice d20} brings many surprises to the game—surprises that the DM then interprets.

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: It's a book written in Common called {@i On the Habitations of the Divine in the Celestial and Infernal Realms}.

items.name: Russell:
items.entry: Did you just make that up?

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: I'll never tell. As you flip through the book, you notice it's very academic, almost impenetrable.

items.name: Maeve:
items.entry: OK, I put that one back and pull out another.

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: Are Shreeve and Auro doing anything else?

items.name: Amy:
items.entry: I grab the poker and poke at logs in the fire.

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: As soon as you lift the poker, you hear a grinding sound, and the back of the fireplace slides to the side, revealing a room behind it!

items.name: Amy:
items.entry: "Uh, folks? I found something!" Can I see anything in the room beyond?

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: Past the flames and smoke, you see a glimmering pile of coins heaped near a chest.

items.name: Amy:
items.entry: Anybody have a quick way to put out a fire?

items.name: Phillip:
items.entry: And you laughed at me for preparing Create or Destroy Water! I clutch my Holy Symbol and cast the spell, drenching the fireplace.

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: What does the spell's description say?

items.name: Phillip:
items.entry: It causes 10 gallons of water to rain down in a 30-foot Cube, extinguishing flames there.

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: Great! That puts out the fire. Without the light from the hearth, you're back to the magic glow of Shreeve's sword, which casts your shadows into the room beyond. But you can see, through clouds of lingering smoke, a closed chest on the floor, surrounded by piles of coins. There are two torch sconces on the far wall—one holding an unlit torch with an intricate metal base, the other empty. A skeleton in broken plate armor is lying against that wall, with one hand at its throat and the other holding the matching torch from the empty sconce.

items.name: Amy:
items.entry: I check out the chest!

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: And the rest of you?

items.name: Phillip:
items.entry: Gareth enters and looks at the skeleton.

items.name: Maeve:
items.entry: I keep watch on this side of the fireplace.

items.name: Russell:
items.entry: I'm still back by the first door.

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: Amy, the chest seems expertly made, with elegant fittings and clawed feet.

items.name: Amy:
items.entry: I try to open it. Is it locked?

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: It's not locked and opens easily—and it releases a cloud of sweet-smelling gas.

items.name: Amy:
items.entry: Oh, no.

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: Oh, yes. I need Auro and Gareth to make Constitution saving throws.

items.name: Amy:
items.entry: Sorry, Phillip! I got an 8.

items.name: Phillip:
items.entry: And a 5 for Gareth.

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: As you draw this gas into your lungs, you feel a chill grip you, and your bodies stiffen. You both have the Paralyzed condition!

entries.name: (4)—Finding Hidden Objects
entries: Adventure environments are full of secrets: traps, concealed doors, loose floorboards, and hidden treasures. Characters often use Wisdom checks to find things—see the {@action Search|XPHB} action in the {@area rules glossary|a8f|x}—but sometimes they stumble on them accidentally, as Auro did here.

entries.name: (5)—Casting Spells
entries: Many characters have the ability to cast spells, which have a huge variety of effects. Some spells are mostly useful in combat, by dealing damage or imposing conditions. Other spells have utility in exploration. If you're playing a spellcaster, look for a mix of combat-effective and utilitarian spells to help deal with varied challenges.

entries.name: Know Your Spells!
entries: Have your Player's Handbook open to the description of a spell before you cast it. Don't expect the DM to know how your spell works, and be ready to answer any questions about it.

entries.name: (6)—Vision and Light
entries: The DM determines what the adventurers can perceive, which means being aware of light sources—like the leaping flames in the fireplace and Shreeve's glowing sword—as well as obscuring factors like smoke and fog. See "{@area Vision and Light|04d|x}" earlier in this chapter for more information.

entries.name: (7)—Saving Throws
entries: A saving throw is used to see whether a creature avoids or resists something. When the chest releases toxic gas, Phillip's and Amy's characters make Constitution saving throws. Constitution is one of the six abilities that measure creatures' capabilities, and it has to do with health and stamina. When they fail their saves, the gas causes them to have the {@condition Paralyzed|XPHB} condition. See "{@area Conditions|0b5|x}" later in this chapter for more information.

entries.name: Combat
entries: Adventurers encounter many dangerous monsters and nefarious villains. In those moments, combat often breaks out.

entries.name: The Order of Combat
entries: A typical combat encounter is a clash between two sides: a flurry of weapon swings, feints, parries, footwork, and spellcasting. The game organizes combat into a cycle of rounds and turns. A round represents about 6 seconds in the game world. During a round, each participant in a battle takes a turn. The order of turns is determined at the beginning of combat when everyone rolls {@variantrule Initiative|XPHB}. Once everyone has taken a turn, the fight continues to the next round if neither side is defeated.

entries.name: Combat Step by Step
entries: Combat unfolds in these steps:

items.name: Establish Positions
items.entry: The Dungeon Master determines where all the characters and monsters are located. Given the adventurers' marching order or their stated positions in the room or other location, the DM figures out where the adversaries are—how far away and in what direction.

items.name: Roll Initiative
items.entry: Everyone involved in the combat encounter rolls {@variantrule Initiative|XPHB}, determining the order of combatants' turns.

items.name: Take Turns
items.entry: Each participant in the battle takes a turn in Initiative order. When everyone involved in the combat has had a turn, the round ends. Repeat this step until the fighting stops.

entries.name: Initiative
entries: Initiative determines the order of turns during combat. When combat starts, every participant rolls Initiative; they make a Dexterity check that determines their place in the Initiative order. The DM rolls for monsters. For a group of identical creatures, the DM makes a single roll, so each member of the group has the same Initiative.

entries.name: Surprise
entries: If a combatant is surprised by combat starting, that combatant has {@variantrule Disadvantage|XPHB} on their Initiative roll. For example, if an ambusher starts combat while hidden from a foe who is unaware that combat is starting, that foe is surprised.

entries.name: Initiative Order
entries: A combatant's check total is called their Initiative count, or Initiative for short. The DM ranks the combatants, from highest to lowest Initiative. This is the order in which they act during each round. The Initiative order remains the same from round to round.

entries.name: Ties
entries: If a tie occurs, the DM decides the order among tied monsters, and the players decide the order among tied characters. The DM decides the order if the tie is between a monster and a player character.

entries.name: Your Turn
entries: On your turn, you can move a distance up to your {@variantrule Speed|XPHB} and take one action. You decide whether to move first or take your action first.

The main actions you can take are listed in "{@area Actions|03e|x}" earlier in this chapter. A character's features and a monster's stat block also provide action options. "{@area Movement and Position|077|x}" later in this chapter gives the rules for movement.

entries.name: Communicating
entries: You can communicate however you are able—through brief utterances and gestures—as you take your turn. Doing so uses neither your action nor your move.
Extended communication, such as a detailed explanation of something or an attempt to persuade a foe, requires an action. The Influence action is the main way you try to influence a monster.

entries.name: Interacting with Things
entries: You can interact with one object or feature of the environment for free, during either your move or action. For example, you could open a door during your move as you stride toward a foe.

If you want to interact with a second object, you need to take the {@action Utilize|XPHB} action. Some magic items and other special objects always require an action to use, as stated in their descriptions.

The DM might require you to use an action for any of these activities when it needs special care or when it presents an unusual obstacle. For instance, the DM might require you to take the {@action Utilize|XPHB} action to open a stuck door or turn a crank to lower a drawbridge.

entries.name: Doing Nothing on Your Turn
entries: You can forgo moving, taking an action, or doing anything at all on your turn. If you can't decide what to do, consider taking the defensive {@action Dodge|XPHB} action or the {@action Ready|XPHB} action to delay acting.

entries.name: Ending Combat
entries: Combat ends when one side or the other is defeated, which can mean the creatures are killed or knocked out or have surrendered or fled. Combat can also end when both sides agree to end it.

entries.name: Movement and Position

entries.title: Creatures occupy spaces of varying sizes. This Displacer Beast occupies a 10-by-10-foot space, while the adventurers occupy 5-by-5-foot spaces

entries: On your turn, you can move a distance equal to your {@variantrule Speed|XPHB} or less. Or you can decide not to move.

Your movement can include {@variantrule climbing|XPHB}, {@variantrule crawling|XPHB}, {@variantrule jumping|XPHB}, and {@variantrule swimming|XPHB} (each explained in the {@area rules glossary|a8f|x}). These different modes of movement can be combined with your regular movement, or they can constitute your entire move.
However you're moving with your Speed, you deduct the distance of each part of your move from it until it is used up or until you are done moving, whichever comes first.

A character's Speed is determined during character creation. A monster's Speed is noted in the monster's stat block. See the {@area rules glossary|a8f|x} for more about Speed as well as about special speeds, such as a {@variantrule Climb Speed|XPHB}, {@variantrule Fly Speed|XPHB}, or {@variantrule Swim Speed|XPHB}.

entries.name: Difficult Terrain
entries: Combatants are often slowed down by Difficult Terrain. Low furniture, rubble, undergrowth, steep stairs, snow, and shallow bogs are examples of Difficult Terrain.
Every foot of movement in Difficult Terrain costs 1 extra foot, even if multiple things in a space count as Difficult Terrain.

entries.name: Playing on a Grid
entries: If you play using a square grid and miniatures or other tokens, follow these rules.

entries.name: Squares
entries: Each square represents 5 feet.

entries.name: Speed
entries: Rather than moving foot by foot, move square by square on the grid, using your Speed in 5-foot segments. You can translate your Speed into squares by dividing it by 5. For example, a Speed of 30 feet translates into 6 squares. If you use a grid often, consider writing your Speed in squares on your character sheet.

entries.name: Entering a Square
entries: To enter a square, you must have enough movement left to pay for entering. It costs 1 square of movement to enter an unoccupied square that's adjacent to your space (orthogonally or diagonally adjacent). A square of Difficult Terrain costs 2 squares to enter. Other effects might make a square cost even more.

entries.name: Corners
entries: Diagonal movement can't cross the corner of a wall, a large tree, or another terrain feature that fills its space.

entries.name: Ranges
entries: To determine the range on a grid between two things—whether creatures or objects—count squares from a square adjacent to one of them and stop counting in the space of the other one. Count by the shortest route.

entries.name: Breaking Up Your Move
entries: You can break up your move, using some of its movement before and after any action, Bonus Action, or Reaction you take on the same turn. For example, if you have a Speed of 30 feet, you could go 10 feet, take an action, and then go 20 feet.

entries.name: Dropping Prone
entries: On your turn, you can give yourself the {@condition Prone|XPHB} condition without using an action or any of your Speed, but you can't do so if your Speed is 0.

entries.name: Creature Size
entries: A creature belongs to a size category, which determines the width of the square space the creature occupies on a map, as shown on the Creature Size and Space table. That table lists the sizes from smallest (Tiny) to largest (Gargantuan). A creature's space is the area that it effectively controls in combat and the area it needs to fight effectively.
A character's size is determined by species, and a monster's size is specified in the monster's stat block.

entries.name: Moving around Other Creatures
entries: During your move, you can pass through the space of an ally, a creature that has the {@condition Incapacitated|XPHB} condition, a Tiny creature, or a creature that is two sizes larger or smaller than you.
Another creature's space is {@variantrule Difficult Terrain|XPHB} for you unless that creature is Tiny or your ally.

You can't willingly end a move in a space occupied by another creature. If you somehow end a turn in a space with another creature, you have the {@condition Prone|XPHB} condition unless you are Tiny or are of a larger size than the other creature.

entries.name: Making an Attack
entries: When you take the {@action Attack|XPHB} action, you make an attack. Some other actions, Bonus Actions, and Reactions also let you make an attack. Whether you strike with a Melee weapon, fire a Ranged weapon, or make an attack roll as part of a spell, an attack has the following structure:

items.name: Choose a Target
items.entry: Pick a target within your attack's range: a creature, an object, or a location.

items.name: Determine Modifiers
items.entry: The DM determines whether the target has {@variantrule Cover|XPHB} (see the next section) and whether you have {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} or {@variantrule Disadvantage|XPHB} against the target. In addition, spells, special abilities, and other effects can apply penalties or bonuses to your attack roll.

items.name: Resolve the Attack
items.entry: Make the attack roll, as detailed earlier in this chapter. On a hit, you roll damage unless the particular attack has rules that specify otherwise. Some attacks cause special effects in addition to or instead of damage.

entries.name: Cover
entries: Walls, trees, creatures, and other obstacles can provide cover, making a target more difficult to harm. As detailed in the Cover table, there are three degrees of cover, each of which gives a different benefit to a target.

A target can benefit from cover only when an attack or other effect originates on the opposite side of the cover. If a target is behind multiple sources of cover, only the most protective degree of cover applies; the degrees aren't added together. For example, if a target is behind a creature that gives {@variantrule Cover|XPHB|Half Cover} and a tree trunk that gives {@variantrule Cover|XPHB|Three-Quarters Cover}, the target has Three-Quarters Cover.

entries.caption: Cover
rows: +2 bonus to AC and Dexterity saving throws
Another creature or an object that covers at least half of the target
+5 bonus to AC and Dexterity saving throws
An object that covers at least three-quarters of the target
An object that covers the whole target

entries.name: Unseen Attackers and Targets
entries: When you make an attack roll against a target you can't see, you have {@variantrule Disadvantage|XPHB} on the roll. This is true whether you're guessing the target's location or targeting a creature you can hear but not see. If the target isn't in the location you targeted, you miss.
When a creature can't see you, you have {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} on attack rolls against it.
If you are hidden when you make an attack roll, you give away your location when the attack hits or misses.

entries.name: Ranged Attacks
entries: When you make a ranged attack, you fire a bow, hurl an axe, or otherwise send projectiles to strike a foe at a distance. Many spells also involve making a ranged attack.

entries.name: Range
entries: You can make ranged attacks only against targets within a specified range. If a ranged attack, such as one made with a spell, has a single range, you can't attack a target beyond this range.

Some ranged attacks, such as those made with a {@item Longbow|XPHB}, have two ranges. The smaller number is the normal range, and the larger number is the long range. Your attack roll has {@variantrule Disadvantage|XPHB} when your target is beyond normal range, and you can't attack a target beyond long range.

entries.name: Ranged Attacks in Close Combat
entries: Aiming a ranged attack is more difficult when a foe is next to you. When you make a ranged attack roll with a weapon, a spell, or some other means, you have {@variantrule Disadvantage|XPHB} on the roll if you are within 5 feet of an enemy who can see you and doesn't have the {@condition Incapacitated|XPHB} condition.

entries.name: Melee Attacks
entries: A melee attack allows you to attack a target within your reach. A melee attack typically uses a handheld weapon or an {@variantrule Unarmed Strike|XPHB}. Many monsters make melee attacks with claws, teeth, or other body parts. A few spells also involve melee attacks.

entries.name: Reach
entries: A creature has a 5-foot reach and can thus attack targets within 5 feet when making a melee attack. Certain creatures have melee attacks with a reach greater than 5 feet, as noted in their descriptions.

entries.name: Opportunity Attacks
entries: Combatants watch for enemies to drop their guard. If you move heedlessly past your foes, you put yourself in danger by provoking an Opportunity Attack.

entries.name: Avoiding Opportunity Attack
entries: You can avoid provoking an Opportunity Attack by taking the {@action Disengage|XPHB} action. You also don't provoke an Opportunity Attack when you {@variantrule Teleportation|XPHB|Teleport} or when you are moved without using your movement, action, Bonus Action, or Reaction. For example, you don't provoke an Opportunity Attack if an explosion hurls you out of a foe's reach or if you fall past an enemy.

entries.name: Making an Opportunity Attack
entries: You can make an Opportunity Attack when a creature that you can see leaves your reach. To make the attack, take a Reaction to make one melee attack with a weapon or an {@variantrule Unarmed Strike|XPHB} against that creature. The attack occurs right before it leaves your reach.

entries.name: Mounted Combat

entries.title: Astride a giant seahorse, a paladin adventures underwater

entries: A willing creature that is at least one size larger than a rider and that has an appropriate anatomy can serve as a mount, using the following rules.

entries.name: Mounting and Dismounting
entries: During your move, you can mount a creature that is within 5 feet of you or dismount. Doing so costs an amount of movement equal to half your {@variantrule Speed|XPHB} (round down). For example, if your Speed is 30 feet, you spend 15 feet of movement to mount a horse.

entries.name: Controlling a Mount
entries: You can control a mount only if it has been trained to accept a rider. Domesticated horses, mules, and similar creatures have such training.

The {@variantrule Initiative|XPHB} of a controlled mount changes to match yours when you mount it. It moves on your turn as you direct it, and it has only three action options during that turn: {@action Dash|XPHB}, {@action Disengage|XPHB}, and {@action Dodge|XPHB}. A controlled mount can move and act even on the turn that you mount it.
In contrast, an independent mount—one that lets you ride but ignores your control—retains its place in the Initiative order and moves and acts as it likes.

entries.name: Falling Off
entries: If an effect is about to move your mount against its will while you're on it, you must succeed on a {@dc 10} Dexterity saving throw or fall off, landing with the {@condition Prone|XPHB} condition in an unoccupied space within 5 feet of the mount.
While mounted, you must make the same save if you're knocked {@condition Prone|XPHB} or the mount is.

entries.name: Underwater Combat
entries: A fight underwater follows these rules.

entries.name: Impeded Weapons
entries: When making a melee attack roll with a weapon underwater, a creature that lacks a {@variantrule Swim Speed|XPHB} has {@variantrule Disadvantage|XPHB} on the attack roll unless the weapon deals Piercing damage.
A ranged attack roll with a weapon underwater automatically misses a target beyond the weapon's normal range, and the attack roll has Disadvantage against a target within normal range.

entries.name: Fire Resistance
entries: Anything underwater has Resistance to Fire damage (explained in "Damage and Healing").

entries.name: Damage and Healing
entries: Injury and death are frequent threats in D&D, as detailed in the following rules.

entries.name: Hit Points
entries: Hit Points represent durability and the will to live. Creatures with more Hit Points are more difficult to kill. Your Hit Point maximum is the number of Hit Points you have when uninjured. Your current Hit Points can be any number from that maximum down to 0, which is the lowest Hit Points can go.
Whenever you take damage, subtract it from your Hit Points. Hit Point loss has no effect on your capabilities until you reach 0 Hit Points.
If you have half your Hit Points or fewer, you're Bloodied, which has no game effect on its own but which might trigger other game effects.

entries.name: Resting
entries: Adventurers can't spend every hour adventuring. They need rest. Any creature can take hour-long {@variantrule Short Rest|XPHB|Short Rests} in the midst of a day and an 8-hour {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB} to end it. Regaining Hit Points is one of the main benefits of a rest. The {@area rules glossary|a8f|x} provides the rules for Short and Long Rests.

entries.name: Damage Rolls
entries: Each weapon, spell, and damaging monster ability specifies the damage it deals. You roll the damage dice, add any modifiers, and deal the damage to your target. If there's a penalty to the damage, it's possible to deal 0 damage but not negative damage.

When attacking with a weapon, you add your ability modifier—the same modifier used for the attack roll—to the damage roll. A spell tells you which dice to roll for damage and whether to add any modifiers. Unless a rule says otherwise, you don't add your ability modifier to a fixed damage amount that doesn't use a roll, such as the damage of a {@item Blowgun|XPHB}. See {@area chapter 6|63f|x} for weapons' damage dice and {@area chapter 7|728|x} for spells' damage dice.

entries.name: Critical Hits
entries: When you score a Critical Hit, you deal extra damage. Roll the attack's damage dice twice, add them together, and add any relevant modifiers as normal. For example, if you score a Critical Hit with a {@item Dagger|XPHB}, roll {@dice 2d4} for the damage rather than {@dice 1d4}, and add your relevant ability modifier. If the attack involves other damage dice, such as from the Rogue's Sneak Attack feature, you also roll those dice twice.

entries.name: Saving Throws and Damage
entries: Damage dealt via saving throws uses these rules.

entries.name: Damage against Multiple Targets
entries: When you create a damaging effect that forces two or more targets to make saving throws against it at the same time, roll the damage once for all the targets. For example, when a wizard casts {@spell Fireball|XPHB}, the spell's damage is rolled once for all creatures caught in the blast.

entries.name: Half Damage
entries: Many saving throw effects deal half damage (round down) to a target when the target succeeds on the saving throw. The halved damage is equal to half the damage that would be dealt on a failed save.

entries.name: Damage Types
entries: Each instance of damage has a type, like Fire or Slashing. Damage types are listed in the {@area rules glossary|a8f|x} and have no rules of their own, but other rules, such as {@variantrule Resistance|XPHB}, rely on damage types.

entries.name: Resistance and Vulnerability
entries: Some creatures and objects have Resistance or Vulnerability to certain damage types. If you have Resistance to a damage type, damage of that type is halved against you (round down). If you have Vulnerability to a damage type, damage of that type is doubled against you. For example, if you have Resistance to Cold damage, such damage is halved against you, and if you have Vulnerability to Fire damage, such damage is doubled against you.

entries.name: No Stacking
entries: Multiple instances of Resistance or Vulnerability that affect the same damage type count as only one instance. For example, if you have Resistance to Necrotic damage as well as Resistance to all damage, Necrotic damage is reduced by half against you.

entries.name: Order of Application
entries: Modifiers to damage are applied in the following order: adjustments such as bonuses, penalties, or multipliers are applied first; Resistance is applied second; and Vulnerability is applied third.

For example, a creature has Resistance to all damage and Vulnerability to Fire damage, and it's within a magical aura that reduces all damage by 5. If it takes 28 Fire damage, the damage is first reduced by 5 (to 23), then halved for the creature's Resistance (and rounded down to 11), then doubled for its Vulnerability (to 22).

entries.name: Immunity
entries: Some creatures and objects have Immunity to certain damage types and conditions. Immunity to a damage type means you don't take damage of that type, and Immunity to a condition means you aren't affected by it.

entries.name: Healing
entries: Hit Points can be restored by magic, such as the {@spell Cure Wounds|XPHB} spell or a {@item Potion of Healing|XDMG}, or by a {@variantrule Short Rest|XPHB|Short} or {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB}.

When you receive healing, add the restored Hit Points to your current Hit Points. Your Hit Points can't exceed your Hit Point maximum, so any Hit Points regained in excess of the maximum are lost. For example, if you receive 8 Hit Points of healing and have 14 Hit Points and a Hit Point maximum of 20, you regain 6 Hit Points, not 8.

entries.name: Dropping to 0 Hit Points
entries: When a creature drops to 0 Hit Points, it either dies outright or falls {@condition Unconscious|XPHB}, as explained below.

entries.name: Instant Death
entries: Here are the main ways a creature can die instantly.

entries.name: Monster Death
entries: A monster dies the instant it drops to 0 Hit Points, although a Dungeon Master can ignore this rule for an individual monster and treat it like a character.

entries.name: Hit Point Maximum of 0
entries: A creature dies if its Hit Point maximum reaches 0. Certain effects drain life energy, reducing a creature's Hit Point maximum.

entries.name: Massive Damage
entries: When damage reduces a character to 0 Hit Points and damage remains, the character dies if the remainder equals or exceeds their Hit Point maximum. For example, if your character has a Hit Point maximum of 12, currently has 6 Hit Points, and takes 18 damage, the character drops to 0 Hit Points, but 12 damage remains. The character then dies, since 12 equals their Hit Point maximum.

entries.name: Character Demise
entries: If your character dies, others might find a magical way to revive your character, such as with the {@spell Raise Dead|XPHB} spell. Or talk with the DM about making a new character to join the group. The {@area rules glossary|a8f|x} has more information on being {@variantrule dead|XPHB}.

entries.name: Falling Unconscious
entries: If you reach 0 Hit Points and don't die instantly, you have the {@condition Unconscious|XPHB} condition until you regain any Hit Points, and you now face making {@variantrule Death Saving Throw|XPHB|Death Saving Throws} (see below).

entries.name: Knocking Out a Creature
entries: When you would reduce a creature to 0 Hit Points with a melee attack, you can instead reduce the creature to 1 Hit Point and give it the {@condition Unconscious|XPHB} condition. It then starts a {@variantrule Short Rest|XPHB}, at the end of which that condition ends on it. The condition ends early if the creature regains any Hit Points or if someone takes an action to administer first aid to it, making a successful {@dc 10} Wisdom ({@skill Medicine|XPHB}) check.

entries.name: Death Saving Throws
entries: Whenever you start your turn with 0 Hit Points, you must make a Death Saving Throw to determine whether you creep closer to death or hang on to life. Unlike other saving throws, this one isn't tied to an ability score. You're in the hands of fate now.

entries.name: Three Successes/Failures
entries: Roll {@dice 1d20}. If the roll is 10 or higher, you succeed. Otherwise, you fail. A success or failure has no effect by itself. On your third success, you become {@variantrule Stable|XPHB} (see "Stabilizing a Character" below). On your third failure, you die.
The successes and failures don't need to be consecutive; keep track of both until you collect three of a kind. The number of both is reset to zero when you regain any Hit Points or become Stable.

entries.name: Rolling a 1 or 20
entries: When you roll a 1 on the {@dice d20} for a Death Saving Throw, you suffer two failures. If you roll a 20 on the {@dice d20}, you regain 1 Hit Point.

entries.name: Damage at 0 Hit Points
entries: If you take any damage while you have 0 Hit Points, you suffer a Death Saving Throw failure. If the damage is from a Critical Hit, you suffer two failures instead. If the damage equals or exceeds your Hit Point maximum, you die.

entries.name: Stabilizing a Character
entries: You can take the {@action Help|XPHB} action to try to stabilize a creature with 0 Hit Points, which requires a successful {@dc 10} Wisdom ({@skill Medicine|XPHB}) check.

A Stable creature doesn't make {@variantrule Death Saving Throw|XPHB|Death Saving Throws} even though it has 0 Hit Points, but it still has the {@condition Unconscious|XPHB} condition. If the creature takes damage, it stops being Stable and starts making {@variantrule Death Saving Throw|XPHB|Death Saving Throws} again. A Stable creature that isn't healed regains 1 Hit Point after {@dice 1d4} hours.

entries.name: Temporary Hit Points
entries: Some spells and other effects confer Temporary Hit Points, which are a buffer against losing actual Hit Points, as explained below.

entries.name: Lose Temporary Hit Points First
entries: If you have Temporary Hit Points and take damage, those points are lost first, and any leftover damage carries over to your Hit Points. For example, if you have 5 Temporary Hit Points and take 7 damage, you lose those points and then lose 2 Hit Points.

entries.name: Duration
entries: Temporary Hit Points last until they're depleted or you finish a {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB}.

entries.name: Temporary Hit Points Don't Stack
entries: Temporary Hit Points can't be added together. If you have Temporary Hit Points and receive more of them, you decide whether to keep the ones you have or to gain the new ones. For example, if a spell grants you 12 Temporary Hit Points when you already have 10, you can have 12 or 10, not 22.

entries.name: They're Not Hit Points or Healing
entries: Temporary Hit Points can't be added to your Hit Points, healing can't restore them, and receiving Temporary Hit Points doesn't count as healing. Because Temporary Hit Points aren't Hit Points, a creature can be at full Hit Points and receive Temporary Hit Points.
If you have 0 Hit Points, receiving Temporary Hit Points doesn't restore you to consciousness. Only true healing can save you.

entries.name: Conditions
entries: Many effects impose a condition, a temporary state that alters the recipient's capabilities. The following conditions are defined in the {@area rules glossary|a8f|x}:
The definition of a condition specifies what happens to its recipient while affected by it, and some conditions apply other conditions.

entries.name: Duration
entries: A condition lasts either for a duration specified by the effect that imposed the condition or until the condition is countered (the {@condition Prone|XPHB} condition is countered by standing up, for example).

entries.name: Conditions Don't Stack
entries: If multiple effects impose the same condition on you, each instance of the condition has its own duration, but the condition's effects don't get worse. Either you have a condition or you don't. The {@condition Exhaustion|XPHB} condition is an exception; its effects get worse if you have the condition and receive it again.

entries.name: Combat and Damage Example
entries: In this scene, threats force a group of adventurers into battle. This example demonstrates the turn-based flow of combat that gives each player a chance to detail what they do during the high-stakes moments of a fight.
{@i Below Castle Ravenloft, the characters enter combat!}

items.name: Jared (as DM):
items.entry: Yellow lichen covers the ceiling in this passage, which has alcoves along both sides.

items.name: Russell (as Shreeve):
items.entry: I peer into the nearest alcoves.

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: They each contain human skeletal remains. The silence is broken suddenly by the rattle of bones as the skeletons lurch to their feet all around you and prepare to attack!

items.name: Russell:
items.entry: Ack! How many skeletons?

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: Ten in all, and they're hostile. Roll Initiative!

items.name: Russell:
items.entry: Ten skeletons? Yikes! I got a 16.

items.name: Maeve (as Mirabella):
items.entry: I got 8.

items.name: Phillip (as Gareth):
items.entry: An incredible 2 for Gareth.

items.name: Amy (as Auro):
items.entry: I got a 19!

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: The Rogue is quick to react—but not as quick as the skeletons! They got a 20. The first four attack the person in the lead: Shreeve.

items.name: Russell:
items.entry: Oh, boy.

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: Their attack roll totals are 8, 16, 18, and 20.

items.name: Russell:
items.entry: The 8 and 16 miss my AC, but the others hit.

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: Two of them stick you with their broken blades, dealing a total of 9 Piercing damage.

items.name: Russell:
items.entry: Is that the best you can do?

items.name: Phillip:
items.entry: Never say that to the DM.

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: Heh. Now two of them attack Auro. The first roll is a natural 1: a miss. The second roll is 16.

items.name: Amy:
items.entry: That hits.

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: You take 4 Piercing damage, and one of them attacks Mirabella with a roll of 14.

items.name: Maeve:
items.entry: Hits. No, wait! I cast Shield, so that misses.

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: The skeleton's blade bounces off your shield of magical force. Then two of them attack Gareth. One misses with a 5, but the other one lands a solid blow with a 21, dealing 7 piercing damage.

items.name: Phillip:
items.entry: That got my attention!

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: That's nine attacks. There's one more skeleton at the end of the hall. It moves up and waits for an opening. Now it's Auro's turn.

items.name: Amy:
items.entry: I attack one close to me. Does a 24 hit?

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: A solid hit!

items.name: Amy:
items.entry: And it's next to one of my allies, right?

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: Yes.

items.name: Amy:
items.entry: So with my Sneak Attack, that's 22 damage!

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: Your blade slides into an empty eye socket, and the skeleton clatters to the ground, now inanimate and harmless.

items.name: Amy:
items.entry: Then I use Cunning Action to Disengage as a Bonus Action and move 20 feet out of the melee.

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: Very good. Shreeve?

items.name: Russell:
items.entry: I drop my sword and pull out my warhammer. Time to break some bones! My first attack is a 21 to hit for 7 Bludgeoning damage.

entries.name: (8)—Starting Combat
entries: While describing the skeletons animating, the DM gets ready to start combat by mentally figuring out where everyone is, referring to the map of the area and the party's established marching order.

entries.name: (9)—Rolling Initiative
entries: The next step in combat is for everyone involved to roll {@variantrule Initiative|XPHB}.

entries.name: (10)—Taking Turns
entries: Now each participant in the battle takes a turn in Initiative order. The skeletons go first because they got the highest Initiative: 20.

entries.name: (11)—Attack Rolls
entries: When a creature attacks, whether swinging a sword or firing an arrow from a bow, its player makes an attack roll. If the total is equal to or higher than the target's {@variantrule Armor Class|XPHB} (AC), the attack hits.

entries.name: (12)—Spells and Reactions
entries: Mirabella casts the {@spell Shield|XPHB} spell. It's a special property of this spell that it can be cast even when it's not the caster's turn, using her Reaction (see "{@area Actions|041|x}" earlier in this chapter).

entries.name: (13)—Special Abilities
entries: Auro's Sneak Attack lets him deal extra damage to the skeletons, and his Cunning Action lets him {@action Disengage|XPHB} as a Bonus Action. These are examples of class features (described in {@area chapter 3|119|x}) that let characters bend the rules.

entries.name: (14)—Vulnerability
entries: An attack that deals Bludgeoning damage is deadly to skeletons. Shreeve knows this from past experience, which is why she drops her sword and switches to a Bludgeoning weapon. She rolls only 7 damage, but the DM knows the skeleton actually takes 14 damage.

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: It tries to block your swing, but the force of your blow destroys the skeleton!

items.name: Russell:
items.entry: I swing at the next skeleton with 11 to hit.

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: The skeleton dodges out of the way.

items.name: Russell:
items.entry: Rats. That's my turn.

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: Mirabella?

items.name: Maeve:
items.entry: How many can I get in a 15-foot Cube?

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: Three if you don't want to get Shreeve too.

items.name: Maeve:
items.entry: That's probably best. I cast Thunderwave at those three, using a level 2 spell slot. So there's a loud boom, and a wave of thunderous force sweeps over the skeletons. They need to make {@dc 15} Constitution saves.

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: They all fail!

items.name: Maeve:
items.entry: Because I used a level 2 slot, that's 15 Thunder damage, and they're pushed 10 feet away.

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: They're pushed back and shattered.

items.name: Maeve:
items.entry: Excellent! Four down, six to go.

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: And it's Gareth's turn at last!

items.name: Phillip:
items.entry: How many of them are within 30 feet of me?

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: All six.

items.name: Phillip:
items.entry: I hold up my Holy Symbol and ask Pelor the Holy Sun to sear these skeletons. They need to make {@dc 15} Wisdom saves.

items.name: Jared (rolling):
items.entry: Oh, those are not good numbers. None of them even got close.

items.name: Phillip:
items.entry: They each take 18 Radiant damage and—

items.name: Jared:
items.entry: Never mind the "and." Pelor does indeed smite these skeletons! They're silhouetted for a moment in a burst of brilliant light, then they vanish, leaving only their broken swords behind.

entries.name: (15)—Areas of Effect
entries: Spells and many other effects in the game fill a specific area that is defined by the rules, like the 15-foot {@variantrule Cube [Area of Effect]|XPHB|Cube} of the {@spell Thunderwave|XPHB} spell. See the {@area rules glossary|a8f|x} for more on areas of effect.

entries.name: (16)—Saving Throws
entries: The skeletons make Constitution saving throws to resist the {@spell Thunderwave|XPHB} spell. When they fail those saves, they take damage and are pushed, as defined in that spell's description.

entries.name: Damage and Hit Points
entries: The skeletons have 13 Hit Points each, so the spells and attacks in this example deal enough damage to destroy them. If a spell or an attack dealt less than 13 damage, the DM would keep track of the damage each skeleton has taken until it is reduced to 0 Hit Points and is destroyed.

entries.name: (17)—Saving Throws
entries: Gareth's Sear Undead is a class feature (see {@area chapter 3|119|x}). As with Mirabella's {@spell Thunderwave|XPHB} spell, Sear Undead forces the skeletons to make a saving throw.
